title: CN-lab-02: Connect Network NS to Host
markdown:
# CN-lab-02: Connect Network NS to Host

CN-lab-01 showed you that a fresh network namespace is isolated by default — its own interfaces, invisible to the host and vice versa. That isolation is the whole point of namespaces, but it's useless on its own: a container that can't talk to anything isn't a container, it's a box. This lab builds the first connection — a **virtual Ethernet (veth) pair** joining a namespace to the host — the exact mechanism Docker uses to give every container network access.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Create a veth pair and understand why it's always created as two linked ends
- Move one end of a veth pair into a namespace
- Assign IP addresses on both ends, on the same subnet
- Bring both ends up and prove connectivity in both directions with `ping`

## The veth Pair: A Virtual Network Cable

A **veth pair** is two interfaces created together, permanently linked: whatever goes in one end comes out the other, like a virtual patch cable. One end stays on the host, the other gets moved into a namespace — and from that point on, traffic between the host and the namespace flows entirely through this single virtual link.

| What | Role |
|------|------|
| `veth-host` | Stays on the host — acts as the namespace's gateway/next-hop |
| `veth-ns` | Moves into the namespace — acts as the namespace's own NIC |
| `10.50.0.1/24` | Address assigned to `veth-host` |
| `10.50.0.2/24` | Address assigned to `veth-ns` |

This lab deliberately stays simple: host and namespace, directly connected, same subnet, nothing routed further out. CN-lab-03.1/03.2 build on this to reach beyond the directly-connected subnet; CN-lab-05 connects two namespaces to *each other* without the host in the middle at all.

## Part 1: Setting Up the Namespace

```bash
sudo ip netns add app-ns
```

Same as CN-lab-01 — an isolated, empty namespace, ready to be connected.

## Part 2: Creating and Placing the veth Pair

### Step 1: Create the Pair

```bash
sudo ip link add veth-host type veth peer name veth-ns
```

This single command creates both ends at once, already linked. Right now both live on the host, both `DOWN`.

### Step 2: Move One End Into the Namespace

```bash
sudo ip link set veth-ns netns app-ns
```

`veth-ns` disappears from the host's interface list entirely and now exists only inside `app-ns`. An interface belongs to exactly one namespace at a time — moving it is a transfer, not a copy.

## Part 3: Bringing Both Ends Up

A veth pair only carries traffic when **both** ends are `UP` — one side being down is enough to break the whole link, same as unplugging either end of a real cable.

```bash
# Host side
sudo ip link set veth-host up

# Namespace side — lo first (same habit as CN-lab-01), then veth-ns
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip link set veth-ns up
```

## Part 4: Assigning Addresses

```bash
# Host end — this will act as app-ns's gateway
sudo ip addr add 10.50.0.1/24 dev veth-host

# Namespace end — app-ns's own address
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip addr add 10.50.0.2/24 dev veth-ns
```

Assigning an address to an interface automatically creates a directly-connected route for that subnet on whichever side you assigned it — the host now knows how to reach `10.50.0.0/24` via `veth-host`, and `app-ns` knows how to reach it via `veth-ns`. No manual `ip route add` is needed for this directly-connected case; that comes up in CN-lab-03.1/03.2, where the namespace needs to reach networks it *isn't* directly connected to.

## Part 5: Proving Connectivity Both Ways

### Host → Namespace

```bash
ping -c 3 10.50.0.2
```

### Namespace → Host

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ping -c 3 10.50.0.1
```

Both should succeed. If either direction fails, work backwards through this checklist: is the destination address actually assigned (`ip addr show` on the right side)? Is the interface `UP` on **both** ends (not just the one you're pinging from)? Did you move `veth-ns` into the namespace before or after assigning addresses — either order works, but the address has to end up on the side it's meant to be on.

**Why it matters**: this exact pattern — veth pair, one end on the host, one end in an isolated namespace, both sides addressed on a shared subnet — is precisely what `docker0`/`dockerd` sets up automatically every time you run `docker run`. You've just done by hand what a container runtime does for you on every single container start.

## Conclusion

A namespace goes from completely isolated to connected-to-the-host in five steps: create the veth pair, move one end in, bring both ends up, address both ends on the same subnet, verify with `ping` in both directions. This is the foundational building block for every other connectivity pattern in this module — CN-lab-03.1/03.2 extends it with routing to reach beyond the directly-connected subnet, CN-lab-04 adds NAT so the namespace can reach further still, and CN-lab-05/06 use the same veth primitive to connect namespaces to each other instead of to the host.
